covered.concept: Ancien Regime and Three Estates
covered.why: Foundation for every cause question; must compare estates on privileges, taxes, population for short/long answers.

covered.concept: Economic Crisis and Financial Mismanagement
covered.why: Core economic cause; needs clear link to war debt, taxation inequality, and subsistence crisis for 3–5 mark answers.

covered.concept: Enlightenment Ideas and Philosophers
covered.why: Named philosophers (Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu) and their specific ideas are directly tested; must match thinker to concept.

covered.concept: Political Crisis: Weak Monarchy and Estates-General
covered.why: Explains the immediate political trigger; voting controversy and deadlock are standard short-answer material.

covered.concept: Tennis Court Oath and National Assembly
covered.why: First revolutionary act; significance as assertion of popular sovereignty is a frequent long-answer prompt.

covered.concept: Storming of the Bastille
covered.why: Symbolic start of Revolution; date, cause, and symbolic meaning are all tested individually.

covered.concept: August Decrees and Abolition of Feudalism
covered.why: Shows immediate social transformation; specific provisions (tithes, seigneurial rights) appear in short answers.

covered.concept: Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen
covered.why: Central document; principles (liberty, equality, property, resistance) and articles are quoted in answers.

covered.concept: Constitution of 1791 and Constitutional Monarchy
covered.why: First written constitution; features (separation of powers, limited suffrage) explain why it failed — a common question.

covered.concept: Fall of Monarchy and Republic Proclamation
covered.why: Phase shift to radical republic; September Massacres, 1792 election, and abolition of monarchy are tested.

covered.concept: Reign of Terror and Committee of Public Safety
covered.why: Radical phase core; Law of Suspects, Revolutionary Tribunal, and 'Terror as order of the day' are exam staples.

covered.concept: Robespierre and Jacobins
covered.why: Named figures; Robespierre's role, Jacobin policies, and his fall are directly asked.

covered.concept: Thermidorian Reaction and Directory
covered.why: Post-Terror stabilisation attempt; Directory's weaknesses (corruption, reliance on army) set up Napoleon.

covered.concept: Rise of Napoleon Bonaparte
covered.why: Culmination; 1799 Coup of 18 Brumaire ends Revolution — must state this clearly for 'end of Revolution' questions.

covered.concept: Outcomes: End of Feudalism and Social Change
covered.why: Consequences question requires structured social, political, economic outcomes; this concept aggregates them.

covered.concept: Legacy: Liberty, Equality, Fraternity and Global Impact
covered.why: Standard long-answer topic; impact on France, Europe (nationalism), and world (anti-colonial) must be distinguishable.

covered.concept: Key Figures: Louis XVI, Marie Antoinette, Lafayette, Mirabeau
covered.why: Named individuals; each linked to specific events (Louis XVI → Estates-General/flight/ execution, etc.) for 1–2 mark questions.

modules.capability: Answer any Class 9 board exam question on the French Revolution — including causes (social, economic, intellectual, political), key events in sequence, major figures and their roles, legislative acts and declarations, the radical phase and its end, and the revolution's outcomes and global legacy — using structured, exam-oriented explanations.
modules.why_here: All 17 in-play concepts form the complete Class 9 French Revolution syllabus in the exact chronological and thematic sequence board exams follow. Splitting would fragment the narrative the learner must reproduce in long answers and make cross-concept revision (e.g., causes → outcomes) inefficient for a one-week timeline.
